newsitem.title: UK: Stick to Dayton or forget aid, Bosnians told.
newsitem.headline: Stick to Dayton or forget aid, Bosnians told.

text.p: Bosnia's ethnic communities will only receive a trickle of foreign aid to help rebuild their shattered country unless they start complying with the terms of the Dayton peace treaty, British officials said on Tuesday.

"The involvement of the international community and its agencies in different parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be conditional on the response of those different parts to the implementation of Dayton," one senior official told a briefing.

The officials, speaking the day before the start of a London conference to take stock of the year-old Bosnian peace process, said the nation's Serb Republic and the Moslem-Croat Federation were badly behind the schedule agreed at Dayton a year ago.
"Those (Bosnian) entities that do not follow those requirements will find themselves at a disadvantage when it comes to other areas of implementation," the official said.

The officials said the various sides were hampering freedom of movement, preventing refugees from returning home, committing human rights abuses, refusing to hand over indicted war criminals and not complying with agreed arms control reductions.

They said the policy of conditionality -- linking aid to a set of conditions -- was already hurting Bosnia's Serb Republic, or Republika Srpska, which had been particularly slow in cutting its weapon stocks.

"Of the international aid dispersed so far, the Republika Srpska is complaining that it has only received two percent. That is leaving the Republika Srpska well behind in the reconstruction race," the official said.

NATO has agreed to maintain an armed force in Bosnia for another 18 months to keep the former warring sides apart but the West fears that unless the country is rebuilt quickly, it will fall apart when Western troops leave.
"If there is no regeneration on the economic level, then refugees will not want to go back, people will not have the motivation for reconciliation and peace will dribble away," the official said.
"Establishing a framework for reconstruction is a primary objective of this conference."

Foreign ministers from Europe and North America, Russia, Bosnia, Croatia and Yugoslavia, as well as officials from the major aid agencies, will discuss the problems during a two-day Peace Implementation Conference on Wednesday and Thursday.
They will also focus on improving local policing, insisting the various powers in Bosnia hand over indicted war criminals and finding ways of stamping out human rights abuses.

"Above all, internationally acceptable standards of human rights must apply in Bosnia and Herzegovina and London will concentrate on that area," said the official, but conceded that the West could not force the various sides to act.

"Conditionality is being seen to have an effect on the ground, but unless people want to improve themselves, want international assistance, want a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina, want to be an acceptable part of the European family, you cannot force them to do the things the Dayton prescribes.
"It's political, moral and economic pressure over the years that's going to have an effect, but I think it needs time," the official said.
One theme running through the conference will be that the authorities in Bosnia must take responsibility for their future.
"The international community does not want to be there forever," the official said.
